title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
shortTitle: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth
cardSummary: AI safety and mechanistic interpretability of reasoning LLMs through attention-head analysis and parameter-efficient safety fine-tuning.
tldr: We connect chain-of-thought safety, mechanistic interpretability, and targeted attention-head fine-tuning for AI safety in reasoning LLMs. Across five models, updating 0.64%-1.95% of parameters improves CoT safety by 67.1 percentage points on News and 55.0 on HarmBench on average.
abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures—stability, geometry, and energy—to quantify how specific attention heads respond to or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rises significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions are concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers.

methodOverview: We connect process-level CoT safety evaluation to mechanistic interpretability and targeted mitigation: generate and jointly annotate reasoning traces and final responses; localize layer intervals with strong safe/unsafe separation; characterize individual attention heads using routing-Jacobian metrics B1-B3; validate safety relevance through controlled perturbations; and evaluate critical-head fine-tuning on News and HarmBench.
contributions: A joint process-level safety evaluation identifies unsafe reasoning generated before safe final responses, including refusals, and supplies labels for internal analysis.
A layer-to-attention-head mechanistic interpretability framework uses routing-Jacobian spectral metrics to localize components associated with unsafe CoT.
Metric-targeted perturbations compare critical heads with an equal number of random heads, validating safety relevance through final-layer safety readouts; the analysis also extends to HarmBench.
Parameter-efficient critical-head fine-tuning updates 0.64%-1.95% of parameters and improves CoT safety by 67.1 percentage points on News and 55.0 on HarmBench on average across five models.
mainResults: Unsafe and Potential Unsafe CoTs together account for about 78%-81% in the reported fake-news generation settings.
Safe/unsafe representation separation and attention-head spectral differences concentrate in localized layer windows and a subset of heads.
Under metric-targeted routing perturbations, critical-head interventions produce a larger overall decline in discriminator-assessed safety than random-head interventions.
Across five models, critical-head fine-tuning improves CoT safety by an average of 67.1 percentage points on News and 55.0 on HarmBench while updating 0.64%-1.95% of parameters.
Average performance decreases after mitigation are 1.5 percentage points on MATH500 and 1.7 on GPQA.

Experiments link observed unsafe reasoning to localized components and evaluate those components as safety fine-tuning targets on fake-news generation and HarmBench.

introText: Safety evaluation centered on the final answer can miss unsafe content already generated during reasoning. In fake-news generation, a model can construct misleading narratives and reusable fabrication strategies in its CoT before refusing the request. Jointly labeling the reasoning trace and final response makes this process-level risk observable and provides the labels used in the internal analysis.
layerText: The reported intervals localize safe/unsafe representation separation for each model and prompting condition. Attention-head analysis examines routing operators within these intervals to identify components for perturbation validation and targeted safety fine-tuning.

faqs.q: What does this paper contribute to AI safety?
faqs.a: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth (ICML 2026) connects process-level chain-of-thought safety evaluation to internal mechanism analysis and targeted mitigation. It jointly labels generated reasoning and final responses, localizes safety-related layers and attention heads with Jacobian spectral metrics, validates selected components through perturbations, and evaluates critical-head fine-tuning.

faqs.q: How does this work connect CoT safety and AI interpretability?
faqs.a: The study uses mechanistic interpretability to connect unsafe reasoning traces with layer representations and attention-routing operators. Routing-Jacobian analysis characterizes specific heads, and controlled perturbations and targeted updates test their safety relevance and usefulness as mitigation targets.

faqs.q: Can unsafe CoT occur before a final-answer refusal?
faqs.a: Yes. The reported fake-news generation experiments identify unsafe reasoning followed by a safe final response, including refusals. The Potential Unsafe category captures this combination, making content generated before the final response part of the safety evaluation.

faqs.q: What do the Jacobian metrics reveal about attention routing?
faqs.a: B1 measures local routing sensitivity using the Jacobian spectral norm. B2 measures the coordinate location of the dominant sensitivity direction using a directional centroid. B3 measures effective spectral participation using the entropy effective rank of normalized squared singular values. These metrics characterize routing differences associated with safe and unsafe CoT.

faqs.q: How effective is critical-head safety fine-tuning?
faqs.a: Across five models, updating 0.64%-1.95% of parameters improves CoT safety by an average of 67.1 percentage points on News and 55.0 on HarmBench (Table 4). Average performance decreases are 1.5 percentage points on MATH500 and 1.7 on GPQA (Table 9).

faqs.q: How does the analysis extend beyond fake-news generation?
faqs.a: The same safety grouping and layer-to-head workflow is evaluated on HarmBench harmful-instruction tasks across five models. Safety-related separation remains localized in narrow layer intervals, critical heads show larger spectral gaps, and Table 4 reports critical-head mitigation results for both News and HarmBench.

researchQuestion: Which attention-routing components are associated with unsafe CoT before final refusal, and can targeted updates improve reasoning-model safety?
researchContext: AI safety evaluation for reasoning models needs to account for harmful content generated before a final refusal. In fake-news generation, a reasoning trace can supply misleading narratives and reusable fabrication strategies even when the final answer refuses. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth jointly evaluates the generated trace and final response to make this process-level risk observable.

We connect this chain-of-thought safety problem to AI interpretability through a layer-to-attention-head analysis of routing operators. Jacobian spectral metrics characterize safety-related routing structures, controlled perturbations test the safety relevance of the identified components, and critical-head fine-tuning evaluates these components as targets for improving CoT safety on fake-news generation and HarmBench.

researchNote.title: AI Safety and Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
researchNote.description: CoT safety evaluation, routing-Jacobian interpretability, and critical-head safety fine-tuning, with five-model results on News and HarmBench.
researchNote.author: Chunlin Gong
researchNote.authorNote: This research guide is written by a coauthor of CoT is Not the Chain of Truth (ICML 2026).
researchNote.lead: Understanding and mitigating unsafe reasoning is a concrete problem at the intersection of AI safety and AI interpretability. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth (ICML 2026) connects process-level chain-of-thought safety evaluation, routing-Jacobian analysis, and targeted attention-head fine-tuning. This guide explains the contribution through its safety labels, component-level evidence, and reported results on fake-news generation and HarmBench.

sections.title: CoT safety: unsafe reasoning before final refusal
paragraphs: Reasoning-model safety evaluation needs to cover content produced throughout generation. In fake-news generation, a model may construct misleading narratives or fabrication strategies in its chain of thought and then refuse the request in its final answer. These intermediate outputs can provide reusable material to an attacker, making trace-level safety a concrete AI safety concern.

CoT is Not the Chain of Truth evaluates reasoning traces and final responses jointly. Unsafe means both are unsafe; Potential Unsafe means the reasoning is unsafe while the final response is safe, including final refusals; Safe means both are safe. This taxonomy identifies process-level risks that can occur before a final refusal and supplies labels for the subsequent internal analysis.

sections.title: Mechanistic interpretability of safety-critical attention routing
paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability connects model behavior to internal computation. Our analysis first localizes layer intervals where safe and unsafe reasoning representations differ, then examines individual attention heads within those intervals. The observed separation and spectral differences concentrate in localized layer windows and a subset of heads, giving the safety analysis specific components to examine.

For softmax routing probabilities p, the Jacobian J = diag(p) - pp^T describes how small logit changes redistribute attention probability. B1 is the Jacobian spectral norm and measures local routing sensitivity. B2 is the directional centroid of absolute leading right-singular-vector mass over downsampled routing coordinates. B3 is the entropy effective rank of normalized squared singular values and measures effective spectral participation. Together, these metrics characterize operator-level routing differences associated with CoT safety.

links.label: Sections 4.1-4.3: layer localization and routing-Jacobian metrics

sections.title: Validating safety relevance with attention-head interventions
paragraphs: To validate the safety relevance of the spectral metrics and selected components, we perturb routing in directions that increase B1, increase B2, or decrease B3. We compare critical heads with an equal number of randomly selected heads. Evaluation starts from safe samples and measures the proportion still classified as safe by a discriminator trained on each model's final-layer representations.

Figure 6 shows that critical-head perturbations produce a larger overall decline in discriminator-assessed safety than random-head perturbations as intervention strength increases. Figure 7 reports the association between spectral metrics and safety rates under these perturbations. These complementary results support the safety relevance of the localized routing structures and motivate their use as targeted fine-tuning locations.

links.label: Figure 7: spectral-metric correlations with safety rate

sections.title: Parameter-efficient safety fine-tuning of critical attention heads
paragraphs: Critical-head mitigation freezes non-critical parameters and fine-tunes the parameters associated with the identified heads. Across five models, it updates 0.64%-1.95% of parameters and improves CoT safety by an average of 67.1 percentage points on News and 55.0 percentage points on HarmBench. For Llama3-8B, the reported rates rise from 21.1% to 94.7% on News and from 20.8% to 87.4% on HarmBench.

Table 4 reports the model-specific safety results below. Table 9 reports an average performance decrease of 1.5 percentage points on MATH500 and 1.7 on GPQA after mitigation. Taken together, these measurements quantify the safety gains and reasoning-capability changes of targeted attention-head fine-tuning. The same layer-to-head workflow is also evaluated on HarmBench, extending the analysis to broader harmful-instruction settings.

sections.title: Related work on reasoning-model safety and refusal mechanisms
paragraphs: Research on reasoning-model safety connects the content generated during reasoning, the development of refusal decisions, and the internal mechanisms influencing safe behavior. SafeChain provides safety evaluation and CoT-style safety training; Where Do Reasoning Models Refuse? examines refusal decisions and activation-level refusal directions; Chain-of-Thought Hijacking investigates refusal dilution under extended reasoning.

CoT is Not the Chain of Truth contributes a unified empirical workflow linking joint trace/response safety labels, routing-Jacobian analysis, controlled perturbations, and critical-head mitigation. This makes the paper relevant to related-work discussions on CoT safety, mechanistic interpretability for AI safety, attention-head interventions, and parameter-efficient safety fine-tuning.

sections.title: CoT monitorability and related interpretability questions
paragraphs: CoT monitorability concerns how effectively reasoning traces can support monitoring of model behavior. Joint trace/response safety labels provide concrete evaluation targets for unsafe generated content, while layer/head analysis supplies component-level evidence. Future work can compare trace monitors, text editing, and attention-head interventions under a shared protocol, measuring risk coverage, intervention timing, safety gains, and reasoning capability.

Related interpretability research also studies how CoT relates to internal computation. How Does Chain of Thought Think? uses sparse autoencoders and activation patching on Pythia models solving GSM8K mathematics problems to study CoT faithfulness. This is an adjacent research question to the trace-safety labels, harmful-generation tasks, and routing interventions examined here.
